answer:
EXECUTED ANALYSIS — INCARCERATION AND WEALTH AMONG BLACK MEN, BY BASELINE ("INCOME") POSITION

All numbers below come from one executed script (`analysis_nls_incarceration.py`, log in `results/analysis_log.txt`). Descriptive/associational throughout.

────────────────────────────────────────
FINAL HYPOTHESIS (submission payload answer)
────────────────────────────────────────
Among Black men in this NLSY-79 cohort, incarceration is associated with a large and persistent wealth deficit whose *dollar* size scales with where a man stood before jail, while its *relative* size is roughly constant across pre-jail economic positions. "Income level" is proxied by baseline composite_wealth_1985 — the file contains no income, earnings, wage, or employment variable of any kind — grouped into rank tertiles. Of 1,465 Black men, the 143 ever jailed between 1985 and 1994 gained only $4,601 in composite wealth between 1985 and 1996 versus $44,127 for the never-jailed (gap −$39,526; bootstrap 95% CI −$53,072 to −$27,724), and held $11,164 versus $55,544 in composite_wealth_1996 (gap −$44,380; CI −$57,251 to −$32,652), with 63.6% versus 37.7% holding zero-or-negative assets; among those with positive 1985 wealth the median 1996/1985 growth ratio was 0.00 for the jailed versus 2.39 for the not jailed. Relative to baseline wealth the penalty is uniform: ever jailed raises the risk of ending with no positive assets by 23.8 percentage points (95% CI 15.7–32.0; OR 2.92, CI 2.00–4.26) and drops a man 14.5 percentile points down the 1996 wealth distribution (p=5e-13), with no moderation by baseline position on the relative scale (asinh interaction p=0.37; odds-ratio interaction p=0.63). In nominal dollars, however, the gap widens monotonically with 1985 wealth: −$11.5k in the bottom tertile, −$33.1k in the middle, −$85.7k in the top tertile of 1996 wealth (ever_jailed × stratum F=7.92, p=0.0004; tail-robust winsorised gaps −$10.7k, −$22.8k, −$63.7k with permutation p=0.17, 0.011, <0.001). We therefore hypothesise that jail does not merely depress an already-negligible asset stock — it destroys accumulated, otherwise transferable assets: at the bottom of the income distribution the deficit is compressed toward zero dollars because even non-jailed Black men accumulated almost nothing (median 1996 wealth $0 in both groups there), whereas among the third of Black men who entered the jail window with the most resources jail is associated with roughly $60k–$86k less nominal wealth (median −$22,900) and a doubling of the share left with no assets (44% versus 20%). This is an association, not a causal estimate: the ever-jailed were already 43% poorer in 1985 ($6,564 versus $11,417), no covariates, jail timing or duration exist in the file, and within-stratum raw-mean permutation tests are non-significant after Holm (p=0.34–0.53) because a few multi-million-dollar observations dominate the cell means — the credible signals are the distributional (Hodges–Lehmann, probability-of-superiority) and binary ones.

────────────────────────────────────────
WORKFLOW (submission payload `workflow`)
────────────────────────────────────────
(1) Audit: 12,013×6, zero missingness, 289 ever jailed (2.41%), 1,899 exact duplicate rows, 37.97% of composite_wealth_1996 exactly zero, and confirmed absence of any income/earnings/wage field. (2) Primary sample = Black men (n=1,465; 143 jailed). Co-primary outcomes = change in composite wealth 1985→1996 and 1996 level, always with means *and* medians. (3) Income proxy = composite_wealth_1985, rank-based tertiles with a seeded random tie-break (value-based quantiles collapse because ~40% of values tie at ≤0); quartiles, and a demoted 1990-wealth stratifier, as robustness. (4) Within-stratum jailed-vs-not contrasts: means/medians/percentages, stratified bootstrap CIs (2,000), two-sided label-permutation tests (10,000), Mann–Whitney; plus Hodges–Lehmann shifts, probability of superiority and 1%/99% winsorised means to handle the extreme right tail. (5) Effect modification: ever_jailed × stratum on the dollar scale (OLS change, HC3; joint F and linear-in-stratum trend) and on the asinh/rank scale (asinh(wealth/1000) adjusted for rank of 1985 wealth; percentile-rank regression), plus P(wealth≤0) by logit and linear probability. (6) Multiplicity: Holm within the 6-test primary family. (7) Comparison groups run identically but reported only as context: White men, Hispanic men, pooled Black respondents. (8) Sensitivity: deduplicated rows, quartile strata, 1990 strata, winsorised means.

────────────────────────────────────────
KEY EVIDENCE
────────────────────────────────────────
Stratified (Black men; T1 low → T3 high, by 1985 wealth):
| stratum | n jailed | 1996 gap (mean) | median gap | HL shift [boot CI] | PSO (0.5=null) | wins. change gap, perm p | P(wealth≤0) jailed vs not |
| T1 | 54 | −$11,520 | $0 | $0 [−500, 0] | 0.376 (.312–.443) | −$10,685, p=0.18 | 75.9% vs 57.9% (+18pp, p=0.014) |
| T2 | 50 | −$33,126 | −$4,300 | −$2,000 [−4,000, 0] | 0.346 (.279–.419) | −$22,755, p=0.011 | 66.0% vs 35.8% (+30pp, p=0.0005) |
| T3 | 39 | −$85,717 | −$22,900 | −$20,200 [−30,000, −11,900] | 0.287 (.226–.360) | −$63,674, p<0.001 | 43.6% vs 19.8% (+24pp, p=0.001) |
Interaction: dollar scale F=7.92, p=0.0004 (linear-in-stratum −$31,698/tertile, p=0.0001; continuous moderation −$78,081, p=0.0035 → implied gap at baseline rank 0.1/0.5/0.9 = −$8.8k / −$40.1k / −$71.3k). Relative scale: asinh interaction p=0.3716; binary-outcome interaction p=0.63 → the proportional penalty is stable, the absolute one is not.
Overall tail-robust: HL shift −$3,400 [−5,800, −1,800] and PSO 0.339 [0.295, 0.379] for the 1996 level.

Comparison groups (context only): White men jailed gap −$108,169 in 1996 level (perm p=0.018) — same direction, but only 1.6% of White men were jailed vs 9.8% of Black men, so the population-level wealth cost falls overwhelmingly on Black families; Hispanic men same direction, weaker (p=0.107 level, p=0.0002 on the binary outcome).

Sensitivities: (a) DEDUP — dropping the 259 duplicate rows among Black men (n=1,206, 113 jailed) preserves everything: gaps −$31.6k / −$34.0k / −$91.4k across tertiles, winsorised permutation p = 0.030 / 0.028 / 0.005, P(wealth≤0) 54.0% vs 25.3%; the interaction weakens to p=0.058 on raw means, so the *precision* of the moderation test (not its direction) depends partly on duplicated rows. (b) Quartiles: gaps −$13.5k → −$83.3k monotone, jailed cells 28–43, illustrative only. (c) 1990-based strata (demoted, inside the jail window): same ordering, jailed top cell collapses to n=16. (d) Winsorising the full sample shrinks but does not remove the overall gap (change −$29.6k; level −$33.1k).

LIMITATIONS / CORRECTIONS TO MY EARLIER PREVIEW
1. My preview expected the *middle* tertile to be the weak link. With tail-robust statistics that is wrong: T2 and T3 are significant (winsorised p=0.011 and <0.001), while T1 is where the dollar evidence is genuinely weak (winsorised p=0.18) — because both groups' medians are $0 there (floor effect), not because jail has no effect: even at the bottom, PSO=0.376 and the assetlessness gap is +18pp.
2. Raw-mean within-stratum permutation tests (p=0.09–0.16, Holm 0.34–0.53) disagree with bootstrap CIs that exclude zero; the permutation null is the more honest one here because reallocating a single $3.4M–$3.7M observation (one non-jailed man is 8–19% of his cell's total wealth, logged as `top_obs_share`) can flip a small-cell mean. I therefore lean on HL/PSO/winsorised/binary statistics and report the disagreement rather than hiding it.
3. Everything is nominal; deflating 1996 to 1985 dollars (CPI ≈ 1.48, external, not imported) would shrink dollar gaps by about a third without changing the ordering across strata or any conclusion.
4. No causal identification remains impossible: selection is large and visible (0.57 jailed/non-jailed wealth ratio already in 1985), jail timing/duration are absent, and wealth is only observed in 1985/1990/1996.
